In this section, we fix our notations. We assume that $q\in\mathbb{C}^*$ satisfies $0<|q|<1$. The $q$-shifted operator $\sigma_q$ is given by $\sigma_qf(x)=f(qx)$. For any fixed $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^*\setminus q^{\mathbb{Z}}$, the set $[\lambda ;q]$-spiral is $[\lambda ;q]:=\lambda q^{\mathbb{Z}}=\{\lambda q^k;k\in\mathbb{Z}\}$. blocks.title: Covering transformations
blocks.content:
We define a covering transformation for a second order linear $q$-difference equation.

::: dfn
For a $q$-difference equation $$\label{sh}
a(x)u(q^2x)+b(x)u(qx)+c(x)u(x)=0,$$ we define the covering transformation as follows $$t^2:=x,\quad v(t):=u(t^2),\quad p:=\sqrt{q}.$$
:::

blocks.title: The Ramanujan function and the q-Airy function
blocks.content: There are two different $q$-analogue of the Airy function. One is called the Ramanujan function which appears in [@Ramanujan]. Ismail [@Is] pointed out that the Ramanujan function can be considered as a $q$-analogue of the Airy function. The other one is called the $q$-Airy function which is obtained by K. Kajiwara, T. Masuda, M. Noumi, Y. Ohta and Y. Yamada [@KMNOY]. In this section, we see the properties of these functions. We consider the behavior of the equation [\[qai\]](#qai){reference-type="eqref" reference="qai"} around the infinity. We set $x=1/t$ and $z(t)=u(1/t)$. Then $z(t)$ satisfies $$\left(-\sigma_q^2+\frac{1}{q^2t}\sigma_q+1\right)z(t)=0.$$ We set $\mathcal{E}(t)=1/\theta (-q^2t)$ and $f(t)=\sum_{n\ge 0}a_nt^n,\quad a_0=1$.
